newsitem.title: JAPAN: Protocol to the wind, Russian minister wows Japan.
newsitem.headline: Protocol to the wind, Russian minister wows Japan.

text.p: Boris Nemtsov, Russia's action-minded first deputy prime minister, landed in Japan with a splash this week.
And straight-laced diplomacy seemed to take a backseat to personal flare in the new Russian minister's self-styled mission of revamping of Japan-Russia economic relations.

Visiting Tokyo with an 80-strong delegation to churn up new Japanese investment for Russia, Nemtsov first shocked reporters with the bounding steps he took from the airplane that carried him to Japan on Monday, then wowed Japan's business leaders with sweeping assurances that existing and new yen-denominated investments would be handled with unprecedented levels of personal care by Moscow.
The smiling Nemtsov, who turns 38 in October, even went so far as to offer would-be investors his home phone number.
"If you can't reach me at my administrative offices, reach me on my mobile phone," he told an elite gathering of Japan's business community Tuesday.
"If you can't reach me on my mobile phone, reach me at home," said Nemtsov, who is also Russia's fuel and energy minister.

Selected as the antenna of choice between Russian President Boris Yeltsin and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, Nemtsov hand-delivered an invitation to Hashimoto for a visit to Moscow later this year.
Asked by reporters how the Japanese leader responded, Nemtsov laughed and offered a quip reminiscent of Yeltsin's occasional playfulness with the media.
"The response was very good," he laughed.
"Can there be any other reaction?" he asked.

Nemtsov, keen to illustrate what he felt was a new, more personal relationship developing between Russia and Japan, quoted Hashimoto as saying that he hoped to be able set aside a free day to spend with Yeltsin.

He also noted that Yeltsin, too, was keen to communicate with Hashimoto on a personal level, quoting the Russian president as saying such personal relationships sometimes prove more effective in resolving issues than long, government negotiations.

Nemtsov, along with counterpart First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais, 41, is a key player in the pro-reform government formed in March by President Boris Yeltsin as he recovered from months of illness.

The two have been the driving force in the new government, and with full presidential support appear to have a free hand for now. Nemtsov, who was careful last week in Moscow to sidestep the hot topic of Japan's and Russia's ongoing territorial rift over four small islands of Japan's northern coast by saying it was a question for Yeltsin, also stayed away from politically sensitive topics on his visit, which ends on Wednesday. Asked how soon Russia would pursue a contract it had signed for the development of giant oil reserves in U.N. sanctioned Iraq -- a problem which analysts say helped lead to the derailment of Nemtsov's energy predecessor -- he said: "I believe that depends on the lifting of economic sanctions against Iraq."
Asked whether he favoured an early lifting of the sanctions, Nemtsov said: "Maybe. Maybe."
